import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "RANK(TS_MEAN($vwap * $volume, 20) / (TS_MEAN($vwap * $volume, 120) + 1e-8))" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "TURNOVER_SURGE_20_120" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)
7cffba054d4502c8.factor_description: Implements the Miller (1977) / Scheinkman-Xiong (2003) resale-option premium proxy for the A-share no-short-sale regime. Daily yuan turnover is defined as $vwap x $volume. The factor is the ratio of the 20-day trailing mean to the 120-day trailing mean of turnover, so each stock's short-run turnover surge is scaled by its own long-run baseline; this removes persistent firm size and liquidity differences that would otherwise dominate a raw cross-sectional turnover rank. Because pessimists can only abstain when short selling is unavailable, abnormally high churn marks names whose marginal buyers are optimists and whose prices carry a resale-option premium; as retail attention mean-reverts within weeks, this premium deflates, so HIGH factor values predict LOWER forward returns over the next 10-20 trading days (committed negative RankIC, strongest in retail-driven bull phases). The 120-day rolling mean is undefined (null) until the long history is complete, which automatically nulls the factor for newly listed or insufficient-history stocks.

feedback.observations: This is the first factor admitted to an empty repository (repository size 0), so all comparative dimensions scored the neutral 0.500 baseline; the utility of 0.5458 was pulled above neutral almost entirely by the outstanding overfit-survival score of 0.958 — the in-sample edge genuinely survived out of sample. The pre-registered direction was CONFIRMED: committed negative, measured negative (raw RankIC -0.0170, neutralized -0.0189, Newey-West t = -3.93, exactly clearing the 3.93 multiple-testing bar), with clean decile monotonicity in the predicted direction (-0.71) and a flipped long/short Sharpe of +1.49. Engineering quality is excellent: only 75 symbols (well inside the 50-150 simplicity target), daily one-way turnover of just 0.0431, capacity of 5.1e10 CNY, size correlation of only +0.082, and zero overlap with existing holdings. However, three measurements qualify the victory: (1) the edge is strongest at a 1-DAY horizon, not the hypothesized 10-20 days; (2) stability is weak — RankICIR of -0.146 sits below even the 0.20 'weak' industry bar, with the IC keeping its sign on only 54.6% of days; (3) the edge is regime-concentrated — IC on the worst 20% of cross-sectional days is -0.0758 while on the best 20% it flips to +0.0203. Economically, the factor pays for its own trading 4.5x over (|IC| 0.0189 vs the 0.0042 self-cost bar), but the one-factor book is 5.1x short of net profitability (composite |IC| 0.0170 vs 0.0872 needed) — a book-level property requiring many more independent bets, roughly (0.0872/0.017)^2 ≈ 26 factors of this quality, or fewer but stronger ones.
feedback.hypothesis_evaluation: The core of the hypothesis is SUPPORTED: under the no-short-sale regime, high abnormal turnover (20d/120d surge) marks names whose marginal buyers are optimists, and HIGH values predict LOWER forward returns — the direction, mechanism, and sign all checked out, and the factor cleared admission on its first attempt. But two secondary predictions were REFUTED by the measurement. First, the horizon: the hypothesis said the resale-option premium deflates over 10-20 days as attention mean-reverts 'within weeks'; the measured edge is strongest at 1 day, meaning attention-driven overpricing reverts far faster than the Miller/Scheinkman-Xiong 'weeks' story implies — the 20/120 window pair is likely too slow for where the edge actually lives. Second, the regime: the hypothesis predicted the edge would be 'strongest in retail-driven bull phases'; the measurement shows the opposite — the negative IC is concentrated in the worst 20% of days (-0.0758, four times the overall IC) and flips weakly positive in rallies (+0.0203). The premium deflates hardest when the tape falls (attention collapses in crashes), while in rallies high-churn names keep riding the bubble. The factor is therefore a downside-protection signal: it discriminates well precisely when the book needs it most, but its day-to-day consistency (ICIR -0.146, sign persistence 54.6%) must improve for it to carry a book rather than just hedge one.
feedback.reason: Three measured facts drive the refinement. First, the horizon measurement (strongest at 1 day, not 10-20) says the 20-day numerator averages away the very spike it is meant to capture; a 5- or 10-day numerator should align the signal with the horizon where the edge empirically lives and mechanically increase IC per day. Second, the low RankICIR (-0.146) with 54.6% sign persistence indicates the daily signal is noisy — the right-skew of turnover means single blow-off days dominate the flat 20-day mean and then wash out; log/median/z-score constructions suppress those outliers and should convert the crash-day edge (-0.0758) into a more persistent daily discrimination. Third, the crash-day concentration with a rally-day sign flip means part of the current edge may be a price-reversal artifact of using $vwap in the turnover definition; the volume-only variant tests whether the attention channel (the actual Miller/SX variable) is cleaner. All variants stay strictly inside the same theoretical framework — attention and opinion divergence under no-short-sale — so this is hypothesis refinement, not a direction change. Each proposed factor uses only 2-3 raw features and 2-3 operators, staying far below the complexity thresholds (the current factor's 75 symbols had no overfitting warning, and its 0.958 out-of-sample survival shows simplicity is working). These variants also broaden the operator population beyond the current RANK/TS_MEAN duopoly (LOG, TS_ZSCORE, TS_STD, TS_MEDIAN), which improves repository diversity. Finally, the book-level shortfall (5.1x short of the 0.0872 composite-IC bar) is a property of the book, not this factor: the path forward is to keep stacking low-correlation independent bets within and beyond this family, since each independent factor multiplies book IC by sqrt(N) — at the current per-factor IC, roughly 26 independent factors reach the bar, so both stronger variants AND more distinct families are needed.
feedback.new_hypothesis: Refinement within the same Miller (1977) / Scheinkman-Xiong (2003) framework: the resale-option premium attached to abnormal turnover is a FAST-deflating, crash-concentrated phenomenon — attention surges revert within ~1-5 days, and the negative forward-return edge is strongest in falling markets. Therefore shorter, more robust surge measures should raise both the IC magnitude and the day-to-day stability (RankICIR toward the 0.20 bar) relative to the 20/120 pair. Specific variants to test next, each as a separate simple factor (<150 symbols, one window pair per factor): (1) HORIZON MATCHING — shorten the numerator to match the 1-day edge: RANK(TS_MEAN($vwap*$volume, 5) / (TS_MEAN($vwap*$volume, 60) + 1e-8)) and a 10/60 pair; (2) PURE CHURN — isolate attention from price drift by dropping $vwap: RANK(TS_MEAN($volume, 20) / (TS_MEAN($volume, 120) + 1e-8)), since yuan turnover mechanically rises with price run-ups and conflates the reversal effect with the attention effect; (3) OUTLIER ROBUSTNESS — turnover is heavily right-skewed, so a few extreme days dominate the 20-day mean and destabilize the daily IC; use a geometric/log ratio RANK(TS_MEAN(LOG($vwap*$volume), 20) - TS_MEAN(LOG($vwap*$volume), 120)) or a median-based surge RANK(TS_MEDIAN($vwap*$volume, 20) / (TS_MEDIAN($vwap*$volume, 120) + 1e-8)); (4) STANDARDIZED SURGE — RANK(TS_ZSCORE($vwap*$volume, 120)), the same self-normalized attention concept in one operator; (5) DISAGREEMENT DISPERSION — within the same opinion-divergence theory, turnover volatility is a disagreement proxy: RANK(TS_STD($vwap*$volume, 20) / (TS_MEAN($vwap*$volume, 120) + 1e-8)). Also run a small window-pair grid around the current choice — (5,60), (10,60), (10,120), (20,60), (20,240) — to map parameter sensitivity rather than assume 20/120 is optimal.

59348dedee84eb11.factor_description: Size-controlled Amihud illiquidity premium over a 60-day window, matching the 1-3 month holding horizon of the hypothesis. The first leg is the persistent price-impact cost: the 60-day mean of daily |return| per yuan of turnover ($vwap*$volume), ranked cross-sectionally. The second leg adds the cross-sectional rank of 60-day mean yuan turnover, the long-window dollar-volume market-cap proxy named in the hypothesis. Because illiquidity rank and size rank are strongly negatively correlated, their sum cancels the common size component to first order: if illiquidity merely proxies small market cap, the two ranks offset and the factor is cross-sectionally flat, while a genuinely high value marks a stock that is more illiquid than its size predicts -- the less liquid, structurally under-owned large caps that benchmark-hugging index flows skip. Under the Amihud (2002) illiquidity-premium premise the factor should therefore carry positive RankIC against forward next-several-day to 3-month returns, and it directly implements the hypothesis's own falsification test (premium must survive a size control).

feedback.observations: The size-controlled Amihud factor executed cleanly and is NOT overfit — complexity is low (87 symbols, 2 raw features, 1 window), and the overfit (0.965), stability (1.000) and decay (1.000) scores confirm the measured edge is real and persisted out of sample. The problem is that the edge is significantly NEGATIVE: neutralized RankIC = -0.0152 (raw -0.0174, Newey-West t = -2.87), ICIR = -0.107 (below the 0.20 weak bar), sign persistence only 55.2%, and the factor was not kept. The size control worked mechanically — SIZE correlation is only +0.185 and the raw-vs-neutralized gap is tiny — so the negative signal is genuine residual illiquidity, not repackaged size or noise. Two further diagnostics contradict the hypothesis's structure: (1) the edge is strongest at a 1-DAY horizon, not the claimed 1-3 months, i.e., the 60-day illiquidity level behaves like a short-horizon reversal/liquidity-provision signal, not a monthly compensation premium; (2) the IC splits +0.100 on the best 20% of days vs -0.141 on the worst 20%, a pro-cyclical pattern showing residual-illiquid stocks act as an uncompensated crash-risk exposure that gets dumped in downturns. Book-level utility was 0.5965 with middling effectiveness/arr/turnover scores (0.500 each); diversity scored 0.000 — the size-control leg added no distinct information beyond the plain Amihud factor already held (max correlation 0.235) — and the operator population has collapsed onto RANK/TS_MEAN/ABS (100% of all 5 calls).
feedback.hypothesis_evaluation: REFUTED in its own falsifiable form. The hypothesis explicitly staked the claim on the premium surviving a size control ('less liquid, structurally under-owned large caps'); the size-controlled factor delivers the OPPOSITE sign — stocks that are more illiquid than their size predicts UNDERPERFORM (t = -2.87), and the effect concentrates at 1 day rather than 1-3 months. The 'benchmark-hugging index flows leave alpha in under-owned illiquid large caps' story is not supported: the market's avoidance of these names appears informationally correct in this sample. The rally/crash IC asymmetry (+0.100 / -0.141) reclassifies residual illiquidity as a liquidity-RISK exposure (flight-to-liquidity, in the Acharya-Pedersen / Pastor-Stambaugh sense) rather than a static premium. The plain Amihud level factor already in the repository remains the better representative of this framework; this variant is strictly worse and was correctly not kept. Note that a simple sign flip of the current factor is not viable: |t| = 2.87 sits exactly at the multiple-testing bar, which rises as the search proceeds.
feedback.reason: Three measured facts motivate the pivot: (1) the illiquidity level's edge concentrates at the 1-day horizon — exactly where a liquidity-innovation/reversal mechanism lives and where a 1-3 month compensation premium would not; (2) the crash/rally IC asymmetry (-0.141/+0.100) is the signature of time-varying liquidity risk, which is expressed through innovations and co-movement rather than the slow level; (3) self-normalization (each stock vs its own 60-day history) removes the cross-sectional size level that produced the wrong sign, should decorrelate the signal from the plain Amihud factor already held (fixing the 0.000 diversity score), and exercises a new operator (TS_ZSCORE), broadening the collapsed RANK/TS_MEAN/ABS operator set. The construction stays deliberately simple (2 features, 1-2 windows, ~100 symbols) to remain far from the complexity/overfit regime, and the rising multiple-testing bar (|t| >= 2.87 and increasing) demands a cleaner edge than a mere sign flip of the current factor. Main risk: innovation signals trade more than 60-day levels and evaluation is net of cost — hence the optional 5-day smoothing, with a fallback to a short/long turnover-ratio form (e.g., TS_MEAN($vwap*$volume,5)/TS_MEAN($vwap*$volume,60)) if turnover destroys the net edge.
feedback.new_hypothesis: Stay inside the price-impact/liquidity framework but move from the cross-sectional LEVEL of illiquidity to its time-series INNOVATION: a stock whose Amihud price impact is deteriorating relative to its own history — rising |return| per yuan of turnover — underperforms over the next several days, while improving liquidity (falling impact vs own norm) predicts positive returns (flight-to-liquidity / liquidity-risk mechanism rather than static compensation). First factor: F = -RANK(TS_ZSCORE(ABS($return)/($vwap*$volume+1e-8), 60)); to control turnover, smooth as -RANK(TS_MEAN(TS_ZSCORE(ABS($return)/($vwap*$volume+1e-8), 60), 5)). a115a37a836979e2.factor_description: Net count of near-limit-up closes minus near-limit-down closes over the past 60 trading days, implementing the band-truncation demand-carryover hypothesis on the SH/SZ daily panel. Since instrument codes are not available inside the expression, the two regime bands are covered by disjoint close-to-close return windows: a daily return in [9.5%, 11.0%] flags a close at or within 0.5pp of the 10% main-board band, and a return in [19.5%, 21.0%] flags the 20% band of STAR names and post-2020-08-24 ChiNext names; the +1pp upper slack keeps no-band sessions such as IPO debuts out of the count. Symmetric windows around -10% and -20% define near-limit-down events. A high net count indicates repeated one-sided demand truncated by the daily band, with unfilled limit orders queuing into subsequent sessions while the T+1 rule delays profit-taking, so the factor is committed to a positive cross-sectional RankIC against 1-5 day forward returns. Raw integer count, no normalization; undefined until 60 observations exist.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "RANK(PROD(1 + $return, 5) - 1)" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "REV5_RANK" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)

def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):

Each day, for every instrument, the tail-gain score is the average of the rolling 75th and 95th percentiles of daily returns over the past 20 trading days: with 20 observations the 0.75 quantile is the 5th-largest daily return and the 0.95 quantile the largest, so their average proxies the mean of the 5 largest daily gains (the hypothesis's lottery salience marker). The score is ranked cross-sectionally, then orthogonalized against the same-window (20-day) count of daily returns above 9.5% (the limit-up-day count in the A-share price-limit regime, covering both the ~10% and ~20% limit-up bands) by subtracting the cross-sectional correlation times the z-scored count. The residual has zero same-day cross-sectional correlation with the limit-up count, isolating genuine lottery demand from truncation-driven tail gains. High residual = recently extreme-gain lottery name whose tail gains are not mere limit-up artifacts; under retail lottery demand with no short sellers such names are overpriced, so the factor is expected to carry NEGATIVE rank IC against 10-20 day forward returns, strongest in high-turnover speculative episodes. Hyperparameters: tail window = 20 days, quantiles = 0.75 and 0.95, limit-up threshold = 9.5%, count window = 20 days.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "RANK(TS_MEAN(ABS($return)/($vwap*$volume+1e-8),5) / (TS_MEAN(ABS($return)/($vwap*$volume+1e-8),60)+1e-14))" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "ILLIQ_SHOCK_5_60" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)

import pandas as pd

import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "RANK(LOG($close + 1e-8))" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here

    calculate_factor(expr, name)

def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "TS_MEAN(RANK((TS_QUANTILE(DELAY($return / (MIN(MAX(TS_MAX(ABS($return), 250), 0.1), 0.21) + 1e-8), 21), 231, 0.75) + TS_QUANTILE(DELAY($return / (MIN(MAX(TS_MAX(ABS($return), 250), 0.1), 0.21) + 1e-8), 21), 231, 0.95)) / 2) - 0.5, 5)" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "Chronic_Bandride_Tail_Q7595_SkipMonth_5D" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "TS_MEAN(ABS(REGRESI($close, SEQUENCE(20), 20)) * ($volume / (TS_MEAN($volume, 60) + 1e-8)), 20)" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "Vol_Weighted_Abs_Trend_Residual_20D" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)
